ich.title: Ich (White Spot Disease)
ich.explanation: Small white spots resembling salt or sugar grains, often paired with fish rubbing against rocks or decorations, are the classic sign of ich — one of the most common freshwater fish parasites. It spreads quickly to other fish in the tank, so treat the whole tank, not just the affected fish.

fin-rot.title: Fin Rot
fin-rot.explanation: Ragged, frayed, or disappearing fin edges — sometimes with a white or red tinge — usually point to fin rot, a bacterial infection that takes hold when water quality is poor or a fish is stressed. Improving water quality alongside treatment gives the best results.

low-oxygen-poor-water.title: Low Oxygen or Poor Water Quality
low-oxygen-poor-water.explanation: Gasping at the surface or rapid gill movement almost always points to a lack of dissolved oxygen or a water quality problem, often ammonia or nitrite. Test your water immediately and improve surface agitation or aeration.

swim-bladder.title: Swim Bladder Disorder
swim-bladder.explanation: Trouble staying balanced — floating, sinking, swimming sideways or upside down — usually points to swim bladder disorder. It's often caused by overfeeding or constipation and frequently resolves with a few days of fasting, though poor water quality can also be a contributing factor worth ruling out.

aggression-stocking.title: Aggression / Stocking Issue
aggression-stocking.explanation: Ongoing aggression toward tankmates is usually a stocking problem — not enough space, incompatible species, or not enough hiding spots and broken sightlines for weaker fish to retreat to.

new-tank-syndrome.title: New Tank Syndrome
new-tank-syndrome.explanation: In a tank that's less than 4-6 weeks old, an ammonia or nitrite spike ("new tank syndrome") is the most common cause of fish dying or acting sick. The tank's beneficial bacteria hasn't built up enough yet to process fish waste.

stress-illness-general.title: Stress or Early Illness
stress-illness-general.explanation: In an established tank, prolonged hiding or loss of appetite is usually stress or the early stage of an illness that hasn't shown visible symptoms yet. Test your water first to rule out a quality issue, and keep a close eye out for any visible symptoms developing.

urgent-water-quality.title: Urgent: Check Your Water Now
urgent-water-quality.explanation: A fish that's gasping, not moving, or lying on the bottom or side is a medical emergency and is very often caused by an acute water quality problem: ammonia, nitrite, or an oxygen crash. Test your water immediately and do a partial water change if anything is off.

general-post-mortem.title: After Fish Loss: What to Check
general-post-mortem.explanation: In an established, stable tank, occasional fish loss can happen from old age or causes that aren't preventable. Still, it's worth testing your water before adding new fish, since a hidden water quality issue can silently affect the rest of your tank.

cycling-tank.title: Cycling a New Tank
cycling-tank.explanation: A new tank needs several weeks to build up the beneficial bacteria that break down fish waste before it's safe to stock at normal levels. Test regularly for ammonia and nitrite, and add fish gradually.

stocking-compatibility.title: Checking Fish Compatibility
stocking-compatibility.explanation: Compatibility depends on adult size, temperament, water parameter needs, and tank size — there's no single answer that covers every species pairing. Look up your specific fish species against your tank size, or ask in an aquarium community with your exact stocking list.

cloudy-water-bacterial-bloom.title: Bacterial Bloom (Cloudy Water)
cloudy-water-bacterial-bloom.explanation: White or gray haze is usually a bacterial bloom — a sudden spike in the bacteria that feed on excess waste or uneaten food, common in new tanks or after overfeeding. It typically clears on its own within a few days; testing your water rules out a bigger issue in the meantime.

green-water-algae.title: Green Water (Algae Bloom)
green-water-algae.explanation: Green, pea-soup-colored water is a free-floating algae bloom, almost always caused by too much light (duration or intensity) combined with excess nutrients. Cutting back light hours helps prevent it from returning, alongside a direct algae treatment.

tannin-discoloration.title: Tannins (Brown/Tea-Colored Water)
tannin-discoloration.explanation: Brown or tea-colored water is usually tannins leaching from driftwood or dried leaves — cosmetic, not harmful, and often intentional in some setups. Activated carbon in your filter will clear it up if you'd rather have clear water.

protein-foam.title: Protein Foam / Surface Bubbles
protein-foam.explanation: Foam or bubbles on the surface usually come from a buildup of dissolved proteins, often linked to overfeeding or waste. A partial water change plus more surface agitation clears it, and cutting back feeding slightly helps prevent it from returning.

smelly-water.title: Bad-Smelling Water
smelly-water.explanation: A bad smell almost always means decaying organic matter — uneaten food, dead plant material, or something (or someone) hidden in the decor — or a bacterial imbalance. Do a partial water change, check for anything decaying, and test your water to see if ammonia is elevated.

established-tank-ammonia-spike.title: Ammonia Spike in an Established Tank
established-tank-ammonia-spike.explanation: In a tank that's been running a while, a sudden ammonia or nitrite spike usually means overstocking, overfeeding, a dead fish or plant matter decaying somewhere, or filter media that lost its bacteria (often from rinsing it in tap water). Find and remove the source, then support the bacteria colony while it recovers.

nutrient-deficiency-yellowing.title: Nutrient Deficiency (Yellowing Leaves)
nutrient-deficiency-yellowing.explanation: Yellowing leaves usually mean your plants are running low on nitrogen or iron — common in tanks without regular fertilizing. A liquid plant fertilizer replaces what the water column alone doesn't provide.

algae-on-plants.title: Algae Growing on Plant Leaves
algae-on-plants.explanation: Algae growing directly on leaves points to a light/nutrient imbalance — usually too much light for the nutrients available, letting algae outcompete the plant for what's there. Reducing light duration alongside an algae treatment usually clears it.

potassium-deficiency.title: Potassium or Micronutrient Deficiency
potassium-deficiency.explanation: Holes or see-through patches in otherwise healthy-looking leaves usually point to a potassium or micronutrient deficiency rather than disease or pests. A comprehensive liquid fertilizer typically resolves it within a couple of weeks.

low-light-co2-limited.title: Limited Light or CO2
low-light-co2-limited.explanation: Plants that stay small or barely grow are usually light-limited — many live plants need more intensity or duration than a basic starter light provides. A dedicated full-spectrum plant light is the most common fix.

transition-melt.title: Transition Melt (Normal)
transition-melt.explanation: New aquatic plants often shed the leaves they grew before purchase (frequently grown emersed, out of water) as they adjust to underwater growth. This "melt" is normal and temporary — keep the water quality stable and new growth should appear within a few weeks.
